content: Adverse reactions to trimethoprim have been documented and can vary in severity. Below is a detailed description of these reactions, categorized by system and type: 1. Dermatologic Reactions: Patients may experience itching (pruritus) and exfoliative dermatitis. When trimethoprim is administered at the recommended adult dosages of 100 mg twice daily (b.i.d.) or 200 mg once daily (q.d.) for 10 days, the incidence of rash ranges from 2.9% to 6.7%. In clinical studies involving higher doses of trimethoprim in adults, the frequency of rash was notably increased. These rashes are typically maculopapular (flat and raised lesions), morbilliform (measles-like), and pruritic (itchy). They are generally mild to moderate in severity and tend to appear 7 to 14 days after the initiation of therapy. 2. Gastrointestinal Reactions: Commonly reported symptoms include epigastric distress (upper abdominal discomfort), nausea, and inflammation of the tongue (glossitis). 3. Hematologic Reactions: Blood-related adverse effects include thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), leukopenia (low white blood cell count), neutropenia (low neutrophil count), megaloblastic anemia (a type of anemia caused by impaired DNA synthesis), and methemoglobinemia (a condition where hemoglobin is unable to release oxygen effectively to tissues). 4. Metabolic Reactions: Metabolic disturbances such as hyperkalemia (elevated potassium levels) and hyponatremia (low sodium levels) have been observed. 5. Miscellaneous Reactions: Other reported adverse effects include fever, elevated levels of serum transaminases (liver enzymes) and bilirubin, as well as increases in blood urea nitrogen (BUN) and serum creatinine levels, which may indicate kidney function changes. These adverse reactions have been observed in both pediatric and adult populations, with some variations in frequency and severity. It is important to monitor patients closely for these potential side effects during therapy with trimethoprim.
